result:
There is a specific shade of blue that exists only for about twenty minutes before sunrise. It isn’t the pitch-black of night, and it isn’t the golden warmth of morning. Everything in this light looks dipped in ink and quietude. Streetlights hum with a sudden irrelevance, birds haven’t quite started their frantic daily negotiations, and the world feels entirely, blissfully suspended.

I find myself thinking a lot about these in-between states—the hinges on which our days swing. 

We are conditioned to care mostly about arrivals and departures, beginnings and endings. We celebrate the birth, the graduation, the promotion, the destination. We remember the crash of the thunder, not the strange, breathless vacuum of air that precedes the storm. Yet, so much of existence happens in the hallways leading from one room to the next.

Think of the peculiar peace of a long train ride or a late-night drive on an empty highway. When you are in transit, you are temporarily absolved of the responsibility to *be* anywhere. You have left point A, so its problems can no longer reach you; you have not yet arrived at point B, so its demands haven’t started. For a couple of hours, your only obligation is to move through space, watching blurry trees or mile markers slip past the glass. It is one of the few times the modern mind allows itself to drift without guilt.

Music understands this better than we do. Claude Debussy once noted that music is the space between the notes. If you play every note on a piano simultaneously and hold down the sustain pedal, you don't get a masterpiece; you get a cacophony. It is the rests—the deliberate pockets of silence—that carve out rhythm and melody. The silence gives the sound somewhere to go.

Even our bodies rely on this architecture. Breathe in, and pause. Right there, at the very top of the inhale, before the ribs collapse back inward, there is a microscopic cliffhanger. A tiny stillness. 

It’s easy to resent the waiting rooms of life—the literal ones with their outdated magazines and humming fluorescent lights, and the metaphorical ones where we wait for news, for healing, for clarity, or for change. Waiting feels passive. It feels like wasted time. 

But maybe there is grace in the threshold. Autumn isn't failing at being summer, and dusk isn't a broken afternoon. They are entire worlds unto themselves, rich and fleeting. Perhaps the trick to living a little lighter is learning to appreciate the hallway—to stand in that twenty-minute pre-dawn blue, not rushing the sun to rise, just marveling at how quiet things can get before the day begins.
